list.listitem: Injecting an anesthetic/corticosteroid solution may provide prompt, focal pain relief from noninflammatory, inflammatory, and crystal arthritides.
Candidates for injection include patients whose knee pain persists despite oral or topical analgesics and physical therapy.
While no evidence from RCTs supports the use of intraarticular corticosteroid injection for acute gout, it may be considered for patients who cannot tolerate NSAIDS or colchicine.
Corticosteroid injections temporarily reduce local inflammation, but do not modify the long-term course of chronic arthritis.
Corticosteroid injections improve pain for 1 to 3 weeks, but do not improve knee function or relieve pain over long-term follow-up.
Repetitive intra-articular corticosteroid injections may cause progressive cartilage loss and joint space narrowing.
Injecting intra-articular hylans (Synvisc) and hyaluronans (Hyalgan) theoretically restores the normal synovial fluid.
An old (2006) Cochrane review concluded that viscosupplementation for knee osteoarthritis may be beneficial for pain, function, and global patient assessment, especially 5 to 13 weeks post-injection.
Subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reported that intraarticular injections of hyaluronic acid derivatives do not improve knee pain but increase risk for serious adverse effects.
Despite poor evidence for efficacy, these injections are occasionally used in patients who have failed standard treatments for osteoarthritis.
Viscosupplementation may postpone the need for total knee replacement.
A guideline by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections.

Injecting a concentrate of autologous growth factors from the blood (platelet-rich plasma) theoretically aids in tissue regeneration. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) considers platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection to be an experimental procedure that should not be performed outside of a research context.
Injections of PRP into the knee may improve function for up to 1 year in patients with mild arthritis but do not reduce pain.
Patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis have similar improvement in knee pain and function with PRP injections compared to viscosupplementation.

A high-quality randomized controlled trial of adults with mild knee DJD found no differences in pain, function, or quality of life between PRP and saline injections at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months.

A meta-analysis of 18 mostly low quality RCTs found improvement in pain and function with PRP injection. However, data from high-quality studies only demonstrated functional improvement but no meaningful pain improvement after 12 months of follow-up. Data on adverse events were not reported.
Injecting non-medical irritant solutions, such as 10% dextrose, into joint spaces theoretically promotes healing through unclear mechanisms.
Prolotherapy is a complementary therapy for chronic musculoskeletal conditions.
Prolotherapy injections improve knee pain and function compared to saline injections and home exercises, though the difference may not be clinically significant.
Prolotherapy should be performed by an experienced injector.
Experimental studies on joint injections of fat-derived mesenchymal stem cells show that they relieve knee pain in the short term.

A double-blind RCT from Korea (N=261) found that ultrasound-guided adipose-derived stem cell injection for moderate knee DJD results to clinically meaningful improvement in pain and function at 6 months compared to saline injection. The stem cells were cultured for 3 weeks before injection, which is a practice not routinely done in the US.

Contraindications to injection include cellulitis over the intended entry site, septic arthritis or adjacent osteomyelitis, bacteremia, uncontrolled coagulopathy, joint prosthesis, or lack of response to prior injections.
A relative contraindication to hyaluronic acid is an allergy to eggs or feathers.
Refer to an orthopedist if infection in a joint prosthesis is suspected.
Inform the patient of the risks, benefits, and possible complications of a knee injection.
Wear protective gloves and use sterile technique.
Have the patient lie supine with the knee slightly flexed, supported underneath with a rolled towel.
Palpate and identify the borders of the patella and mark the entry site with a pen (see ).
Prepare the skin with a bactericidal solution, such as povidone-iodine.
Draw up the correct amounts of steroid and anesthetic, and mix well by tipping the syringe back and forth.

Use a combination of 5 to 10 ml of 1% lidocaine or 0.25% to 0.5% bupivacaine mixed with 0.5 to 2 ml of the selected steroid (20-80 mg of methylprednisolone acetate, 20-40 mg of triamcinolone acetate or 6-12 mg of betamethasone acetate/phosphate).
Hyaluronic acid injections come in 2 ml prefilled syringes given once per week for 5 weeks for Hyalgan and once per week for 3 weeks for Synvisc.
May infiltrate the skin with 3 to 5 ml of local anesthetic using a 30 gauge 1 inch needle OR spray ethyl chloride over the planned injection site.
Use a 20 to 27 gauge 1 inch needle on a 10 ml syringe to enter the joint.

For the lateral approach, enter the skin 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superior lateral aspect of the patella; direct the needle at a 45° angle, tilting below the patella, and aim toward the middle of the medial side of the joint (see ).
For the medial approach, enter the medial aspect of the knee at the middle of the patella, aiming toward the lateral midpole.
For the anterior approach, the patient's knee should be flexed 90°; keeping the needle parallel to the tibial plateau, enter just medial or lateral to the patellar tendon (see ).
May feel a "pop" when penetrating the joint capsule. Flow of the injection should not meet resistance.
Change the path of the needle slightly if injecting the medication is difficult; the needle may be within a fat pad or thick synovium.
Redirect or withdraw the needle if severe pain occurs; the needle may be hitting the cartilaginous surface.
Apply a bandage after withdrawing the needle.
In general, complications are rare.
Bleeding into the joint is unusual in patients without underlying coagulopathy.
Infection of the joint space occurs in less than 1:10,000 procedures.
In 1% to 2% of patients, knee pain may increase in the first 12 to 24 hours, called a steroid or postinjection flare; treat with ice and NSAIDS.
Repetitive injections may damage articular cartilage and weaken capsular ligaments; limit injections to 4 per year and allow at least 6 weeks between injections.
Pain relief may be short lived (2-3 weeks) or not obtained.
Corticosteroid injections may cause temporary elevations in glucose levels in diabetics.
Hyaluronic acid injections more frequently cause pain and may produce a large joint effusion or rash and itching.
Allergic reactions are very rare.
Rest the knee.
Avoid strenuous activity for 48 hours.
Bathe as usual.
Report fever or signs of joint infection.
Return if pain persists greater than 72 hours after injection.
